This type of theophoric name (a name containing the name of a deity) was common among Babylonian officials, who often included the name of a deity in their name to show their connection to royal and religious power.
H5562.emploi: Samgar-Nebo appears only once in the entire Bible, in Jeremiah 39:3, during the account of the fall of Jerusalem under Nebuchadnezzar. He is mentioned among the Babylonian princes and generals who take their place at the city gate after its surrender. This unique mention reflects the historical significance of this officer in the events of 586 BC, a decisive moment when the kingdom of Judah lost its independence.

sens: The bud or flower that appears on the vine before the grape forms
The springtime moment when the vine blooms and shows its harvest potential
Figuratively, the beauty and allure of a young woman
H5563.detail:
1. The vine flower is the floral bud that blooms on the vine in spring, before the fruit forms. It is a very brief but crucial moment: if the flowers appear, the grapes will follow. In Song of Solomon 2:13, the poet describes this blooming that fills the air with fragrance, a sign that the season is fruitful.
2. The blooming of the vine marks the beginning of spring and the hope for a good harvest. In Song of Solomon 2:15, the "little foxes" that ravage the blooming vines threaten precisely this promising moment when the harvest becomes possible. It is a fragile and precious instant.
3. Figuratively, the vine flower symbolizes the youthful and radiant beauty of a woman, her attractiveness at its peak. In Song of Solomon 7:13, when one wants to "see if the flower opens," one contemplates the beauty that blossoms, an image of desire and mutual admiration.
H5563.origine: The Hebrew word שְׁמַדֵר comes from a root that specifically denotes what blooms and opens on the vine. It appears only in the Song of Solomon, this great biblical love poem, where the blooming nature is constantly used to speak of love and attraction between lovers. This choice of vocabulary connects human love to the fertility and beauty of creation.
H5563.emploi: The word appears only three times, all in the Song of Solomon, this mysterious love poem of the ancient Near East. It always refers to the flower or bud of the vine, a key moment in agricultural life and also a poetic image of beauty and promise. Throughout the poem, the vine flower serves to celebrate the mutual beauty of the lovers and the season favorable to love. The fragility of this flower (exposed to the foxes in 2:15) also reflects the vulnerability of tender feelings.
H5563.portee: For the Christian reader, this word invites us to see the beauty of the created world and the love between man and woman as sacred and worthy of celebration. The vine flower, fragile and ephemeral, reminds us that beauty and love are divine gifts that deserve our vigilance and gratitude. The Song of Solomon teaches that praising love and beauty is a form of praise to God Himself.

sens: Placing one's hand on something or someone
Resting, putting a burden on
Consolidating, strengthening, giving strength
Sustaining, nourishing, maintaining
Rescuing, helping in times of trial
H5564.detail:
1. Placing one's hand on something or someone: the concrete gesture of the finger or palm that rests. In Israel's worship, the faithful "lays his hand" on the head of the sacrificial animal to transfer his sin: it is a gesture of identification and consecration (Leviticus 1:4). Similarly, Moses "lays his hands" on Joshua to pass on authority and the Spirit (Numbers 27:23).
2. Resting, putting a burden on: supporting something to prevent it from falling or bending. It is the image of physical support, as when one leans on a stick or rests on a support (Isaiah 36:6, "this broken reed of Egypt, which breaks in the hand of the one who leans on it").
3. Consolidating, strengthening, giving strength: making stable, firm, unshakeable. The heart that is "steadfast" fears nothing (Psalms 112:8); it is the soul that regains tenacity in the face of fear.
4. Sustaining, nourishing, maintaining: keeping someone alive, providing for their needs. When Isaac tells Esau, "I have provided him with grain and wine" (Genesis 27:37), he uses this verb to say that he has established and maintained him.
5. Rescuing, helping in times of trial: supporting someone who falters or falls. The Lord "upholds the righteous" when their strength weakens (Psalms 37:17); He lifts them from their fall (Psalms 145:14).
H5564.origine: This Hebrew root sémakh evokes the idea of taking support, of leaning, from which naturally derives the meaning of laying, placing, then supporting and strengthening. The verb has three main forms in biblical Hebrew: the simple form (Qal) means "to lay on, to lean, to support"; the reflexive form (Niphal) relates to the idea of supporting oneself or taking support; the intensive form (Piel) emphasizes the character of sustenance and revitalization. The word is common in the Old Testament and refers to gestures that are both ritual (the laying on of hands in the temple) and spiritual (divine support).
H5564.emploi: This verb appears 47 times in the Hebrew Bible and is used in four main contexts. First, in liturgy: the faithful "lays his hand" on the sacrificial offering during the offering (Leviticus 1:4 and following), a gesture that becomes the heart of atonement in Israel. Secondly, during the transmission of power or the Spirit: Moses "lays his hands" on Joshua to qualify and invest him (Numbers 27:23, Deuteronomy 34:9). Thirdly, in the expression of physical strength: one leans on an object, or a weapon leans on an enemy (Judges 16:29). Finally, in the spiritual and psychological realm: God "upholds" the believer (Psalms 37:17), "strengthens" his heart (Psalms 112:8), or "lifts" him from distress (Psalms 145:14). The verb thus glides from the material gesture to the spiritual reality of divine help.
H5564.portee: This word reveals that the relationship with God in Israel begins with the gesture — the hand laid, the contact established — which manifests the intention of the heart and creates the link between man and God. It also shows that Christian strength is not autonomous: the weak believer is "upheld" by God Himself, who never abandons him in trial. It is a word of comfort: he who leans on the Lord will never be left alone.

sens: A man from the tribe of Levi during the time of the divided monarchy
A son of Schemaeja and brother of Othni, Rephaël, Obed, Élzabad, and Élihu
H5565.detail: Semaeja is a Levite from the lineage of Korah, living during the time of the divided monarchy in Israel. He is one of the sons of the Levite Schemaeja and belongs to a brotherhood of seven valiant men mentioned for their service in the temple (1 Chronicles 26:7). His name, which means "Jehovah has supported," reflects his parents' trust in God's help. Although few details are given about his personal life, his enumeration among the Levitical guardians suggests that he held an important responsibility in temple worship.
H5565.origine: The name Semaeja is composed of the Hebrew verb "samakh" (to support, to lean on, to trust) and the name of God "Yah." It literally means "Jehovah has supported," expressing a parent's trust at the time of the child's birth. It is a typical theophoric name in the Old Testament, where the name borne by the child proclaims God's action or qualities.
H5565.emploi: Semaeja is mentioned only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 26:7, where he appears in the list of the sons of Schemaeja. The context indicates that he and his brothers were valiant and important men, likely porters or guardians of the temple under their father's oversight. His inclusion in this genealogy shows that he belonged to a prominent Levitical family, entrusted with essential responsibilities in the organized worship of Israel.

sens: Image or statue made to represent a deity
Carved or shaped object that men worship as a god
Representation that provokes God's jealousy and wrath
H5566.detail:
1. An idol is an image carved from stone or wood, or sculpted from metal, to represent a god or deity. It is a material, tangible object that can be seen and touched. In Deuteronomy 4:16, it speaks of "the carved image, a representation of some idol, the figure of a man or a woman": it is the concrete object given human form.
2. The idol is what men create and worship as a god, treating it as a divine being worthy of worship and offerings. When King Manasseh "set the carved image of the idol he had made in the house of God" (2 Chronicles 33:7), he transformed an object shaped by his hands into a center of worship.
3. For the God of Israel, the idol is an abominable object that provokes Him to jealousy and anger. Ezekiel sees "the idol of jealousy" (Ezekiel 8:3 and 8:5) placed at the entrance of the temple: it is a sacred scandal that offends the one true God. That is why Manasseh, in repentance, must "remove from the house of the Lord the foreign gods and the idol" (2 Chronicles 33:15).
H5566.origine: The Hebrew word semèl comes from a root that means "to resemble" or "to correspond." The idol is literally what is shaped to resemble a deity. It is a substitute image: a tangible representation of the god one wishes to worship. The word stands in radical opposition to the theology of Israel, for whom God has no visible form that could be imitated in stone or wood.
H5566.emploi: The word appears 5 times in the Hebrew Bible, always to designate an object of idolatrous worship, never in a neutral or merely descriptive sense. It focuses on two contexts: first in Deuteronomy 4:16, where Moses formally prohibits making an idol in any human form; then in the account of King Manasseh's repentance (2 Chronicles 33:7 and 33:15), where the idol placed in the temple must be eliminated; finally in Ezekiel (8:3 and 8:5), who sees in vision this "idol of jealousy" to the north of the temple, a symbol of the abomination that attracts divine judgment. Each time, the idol embodies infidelity to God and a departure from pure worship.
H5566.portee: The concept of an idol denounces a serious spiritual reality: humanity's tendency to create gods in its own image, visible and controllable, rather than submitting to the invisible God. For the Christian, it serves as a warning: an idol is not just an ancient statue, but anything placed before God to which one devotes worship—money, image, self-desire. Keeping God's name pure means rejecting any representation that would dishonor Him.

sens: Determine or fix the place where something is to go
Assign a defined position to something
Organize space by separating areas
H5567.detail:
1. The verb saman literally means to mark or delimit a space: to fix where something is or should be placed. In the passage from Isaiah 28:25, it refers to how the farmer organizes his field by marking the place of each crop—wheat, barley, spelt—each in its own row or area. It is an act of planning and ordering.

2. More broadly, the word evokes the idea of determination or assignment: something deliberate and organized, not random. This implies intention, a will to put each thing in its place.
H5567.origine: The word comes from a Semitic root that expresses the idea of marking or signaling. It is related to the image of tracing or delimiting, as one marks a boundary or area in a space. The form used here is the participle of the niphal stem, which emphasizes the established or determined state rather than the ongoing action.
H5567.emploi: This verb appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Isaiah 28:25. The context is an agricultural parable from the prophet Isaiah: he describes how a wise farmer arranges his seeds according to a precise and thoughtful order. Each crop has its assigned place. This passage uses saman to illustrate order and wisdom in human affairs, and by extension, divine order in creation and providence.
H5567.portee: This word reminds us that order and planning are part of wisdom. The farmer in Isaiah's parable is presented as studious and intelligent: he does not sow randomly, but assigns each seed the place that suits it. For the Christian reader, it is an invitation to see in divine providence an organizing intelligence, and to recognize that our lives, like a well-cultivated field, require discernment and order.

sens: To stand up, to bristle (for hair or fur)
To shiver with fear or intense emotion
H5568.detail:
1. To bristle means that hair or fur stands up on the skin, usually as a result of a strong emotion such as fear or dread. It is an involuntary physical reaction of the body. In Job 4:15, after a spirit passes near Eliphaz, he describes this sensation: "All my hair stood on end," showing the terror that seized him.
2. The word can also describe a shiver, a sensation of cold or trembling that runs through the body, often caused by fear or religious emotion. The psalmist in Psalms 119:120 expresses this: "My flesh trembles in fear of you," conveying how reverence for God produces an involuntary physical reaction.
H5568.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that describes the movement of something standing up or stiffening. The image is that of hair or fur rising from the scalp due to strong emotion. This type of physical reaction is universal and well-known: it is the shiver or "goosebumps" one feels in the face of something terrifying or sublime.
H5568.emploi: The verb appears only twice in the Hebrew Bible. In Job 4:15, it describes Eliphaz's physical reaction to the supernatural vision of a spirit at night. In Psalms 119:120, the psalmist uses it to express his bodily reaction to the reverent fear of God and His judgments. In both cases, the word paints an intense spiritual emotion through its physical manifestation: the body responds to what the soul feels in the face of the divine or the supernatural.
H5568.portee: This word reminds us that our faith is not merely an abstract mental or spiritual matter: it engenders real physical reactions. The fear of God and the confrontation with the supernatural can transform our very bodies. It is an invitation to recognize that our commitment to God touches our whole being, including our senses and emotions.

sens: having hair or spines standing upright on the body
standing up in disorder, all ruffled
having a rough, hostile, or threatening appearance
H5569.detail:
1. The word primarily describes a physical aspect: something whose hair, spines, or bristles stand upright, like a startled animal puffing itself up to appear larger and more formidable. In Jeremiah 51:27, the horses are said to be 'bristled' — likely referring to their manes standing up, which accentuates their terrifying appearance in battle.
2. Figuratively, the word evokes a hostile and threatening disorder: something that stands up irregularly and aggressively, ready to harm. It is the image of a chaotic battle line or a poorly organized but fierce troop.
3. The adjective also carries a charge of hostility: bristled means repelling, frightening by its rough and untamed appearance.
H5569.origine: The Hebrew root denotes the action of standing up, bristling, like hair standing on end out of fear or the spines of an animal. It evokes the stiffness, the upright and hostile appearance of something.
H5569.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible, in Jeremiah 51:27, where the prophet describes the preparation for an attack against Babylon. The nations are called to rise 'like bristled horses' — that is, spirited, terrifying, ready to strike. The image emphasizes both the raw power of the assembled forces and their wild, almost beastly character.
H5569.portee: This word reminds us how the Bible describes the forces of divine judgment: not a cold and abstract act, but a concrete and terrifying power, comparable to raging troops. For the reader, it is an invitation to grasp the reality of judgment and to respect the gravity of the moment when God acts against injustice.

sens: Ancestor of a Jewish family returned from exile
Name meaning 'thorny' or 'bristled with thorns'
H5570G.detail: 1. Senaa is the name of an ancestor whose descendants formed an important Jewish family. This family is mentioned among those who returned from exile in Babylon with Zerubbabel, the governor of Judah. In Ezra 2:35 and Nehemiah 7:38, the 'sons of Senaa' are counted: they form a group of over three thousand people, making it one of the largest families of repatriates. This mention in the genealogical lists of return from exile shows the importance of this lineage in the reconstruction of the Jewish community. 2. The name Senaa carries the notion of something 'bristled' or 'thorny', perhaps evoking the difficult character or tenacity of this family. This type of descriptive name was common in ancient Israel to qualify the traits of individuals or their ancestors.
H5570G.origine: The name Senaa derives from a Hebrew root meaning 'to be thorny' or 'bristled'. The literal sense would evoke something prickly or difficult to approach. In the Bible, the names of ancestors often reflect characteristics or circumstances: giving a child the name 'one who is bristled with thorns' could suggest strength, tenacity, or an untamed character. It is a typical example of Hebrew names that told a story or expressed a quality.
H5570G.emploi: Senaa appears four times in the Hebrew Bible, always designating the ancestor of a large family. In Ezra 2:35 and Nehemiah 7:38, in the lists of return from the Babylonian exile (around 538 B.C.), the sons of Senaa are counted among the first waves of repatriation: over 3,600 men in Ezra, over 3,900 in Nehemiah, figures that attest to the fertility and importance of this clan. In Nehemiah 3:3, the sons of Senaa appear among the workers who participated in the reconstruction of the walls of Jerusalem, proof of their active commitment to the restoration of the temple and the city. One occurrence in 1 Chronicles 9:7 mentions Sallu, a descendant of Assenua (another form of the same name), established in Jerusalem after the exile.

sens: Adversary of Nehemiah during the reconstruction of the walls of Jerusalem
Governor or notable Moabite from Horonaim
Politically and militarily influential man hostile to the return of the exiles
Representative of foreign powers against the Jewish restoration project
H5571.detail:
1. Sanballat is a powerful man who lived during the time of the return from exile, in the 5th century B.C. His name means 'strength' or 'power'. He first appears in Nehemiah 2:10, when he learns of Nehemiah's arrival in Jerusalem; he is immediately filled with 'great displeasure' at this news.
2. He is associated with Horonaim, a Moabite region east of the Dead Sea. Although Moabite, he wields political influence in the region of Jerusalem and holds the power or at least the prestige necessary to take action against the reconstruction project (Nehemiah 4:1).
3. Sanballat actively and fiercely opposes the reconstruction of the walls of Jerusalem led by Nehemiah. In Nehemiah 4:1, it is said that 'he was angry and very indignant' upon learning of the progress of the work. With other enemies, he mocks the builders and tries to dissuade them through ridicule and threats (Nehemiah 2:19).
4. He openly plots: in Nehemiah 6:2, Sanballat and Geshem send messengers to Nehemiah to invite him to a 'meeting' in the valley of Ono, but the text clearly states 'they had plotted to harm me'. His hostility is not merely jealousy, but a political strategy of sabotage.
H5571.origine: The name 'Sanballat' (סַנְבַלַּט) literally means 'Sin has given strength', where Sin is a Mesopotamian moon god. It is a common theophoric name in ancient Persian and Eastern contexts, revealing the religious and political influences of the region at that time. Sanballat represents the foreign powers that control or influence the region after the fall of Babylon.
H5571.emploi: Sanballat appears ten times in the book of Nehemiah, almost exclusively in chapters 2 to 6 and 13. He is always presented as a resolute adversary of the reconstruction project. At first (Nehemiah 2:10), his opposition is visceral but passive. It gradually becomes more aggressive: mockery and contempt (Nehemiah 2:19), anger and irritation (Nehemiah 4:1), then direct plots and attempts at diversion (Nehemiah 6:2, 6:5, 6:12, 6:14). His machinations all fail thanks to Nehemiah's vigilance and divine protection. In Nehemiah 13:28, he reappears in a context of mixed marriage, showing the infiltration of foreign powers through marriage and alliance.
H5571.portee: The story of Sanballat reminds readers that the spiritual and material reconstruction of God's people always encounters opposition, often organized and cunning. It also teaches that the enemy does not triumph through brute force, but through cunning and seduction (attempts at compromise, marital alliances). It encourages believers to remain vigilant, to discern hidden intentions, and to trust God rather than yield to pressure or suspicious diplomacy.

sens: Small thorny plant
Burning bush: fiery bush from which God spoke to Moses
H5572.detail:
1. A bush is a branched, thick shrub often covered with thorns, smaller than a tree. It is the low, dense vegetation found in arid regions. In Exodus 3:2, Moses sees "a flame of fire in the midst of a bush." 
2. The "burning bush" is the extraordinary event where God revealed Himself to Moses in Egypt: a bush was completely on fire but was not consumed (Exodus 3:2-4). God spoke to Moses from the midst of this bush. It is a miraculous sign of divine power and presence.
H5572.origine: The Hebrew word סְנֶה (seneh) simply refers to a bush or shrub. Its exact root is unknown, but it is a concrete noun for a common plant in the Middle East. The Septuagint (an ancient Greek translation) chose a word that would later emphasize the idea of a plant that burns without being destroyed.
H5572.emploi: The word appears four times in the Hebrew Bible, all in passages related to Moses' calling. Three occurrences are found in Exodus 3:2-4, where Moses sees the burning bush and recognizes the place as holy. A fourth occurrence in Deuteronomy 33:16 recalls this event as an act of divine grace upon the tribe of Joseph: "May the grace of him who appeared in the bush come upon the head of Joseph." The word remains linked to this foundational moment in Israel's history.
H5572.portee: The burning bush reveals a God who manifests Himself in unexpected and impressive ways, in the everyday, to call His servants to essential missions. This symbol teaches the believer that God is present in the simplest places, and that His presence transforms what might seem ordinary into a place of revelation and personal encounter.

sens: Steep rock with rocky ridges near Michmash, north of Jerusalem
H5573.detail: Sene is a rocky height characterized by sharp peaks and rocky ridges that served as natural landmarks. It was located in a mountain pass between Michmash and the territory of the Philistines, about ten kilometers north of Jerusalem (1 Samuel 14:4). This rock formation marked one of the two "teeth of rock" that framed the narrow passage through which Jonathan sought to reach the Philistine camp. Its name, meaning "thorny" or "pointed," accurately describes its appearance: a sharp, rocky ridge that is difficult to access.
H5573.origine: The Hebrew word sene comes from a root meaning "thorn" or "pointed," hence the adjective "thorny." It is a geographical name given to the rock for the sharp shape of its ridges, which evoke natural spikes or thorns. This descriptive name was common for terrain landmarks in the ancient Near East.
H5573.emploi: Sene appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Samuel 14:4, during the account of Jonathan and his armor-bearer's attack on the Philistine outpost at Michmash. It is mentioned as one of the two rock formations that delineated the narrow passage (with Botsets on the other side), a geographical detail that underscores the natural obstacles Jonathan had to overcome. This context shows that Sene was a well-known landmark to the inhabitants of the region of Benjamin.

sens: Descendant of the family of Senaah, from the tribe of Benjamin
Leader or notable of Jerusalem after the exile
H5574.detail:
1. Senua is the name of a Benjamite family whose leader, Judah, is mentioned in Nehemiah 11:9 as "second leader of the city" of Jerusalem. It is a lineage that dates back to the time of the exile and the return of the people of Israel. 
2. In the context of Nehemiah, Judah son of Senua holds a civic responsibility in Jerusalem, alongside other leaders: this shows the importance of this family in the reconstruction and organization of the community returned from exile.
H5574.origine: Senua comes from a root meaning "to bristle" or "to stand up" — an image of something that stands erect, that is stiff. This name also appears in the form Senaah (סְנָאָה). The family is associated with the tribe of Benjamin and the context of the return from exile after the Babylonian captivity.
H5574.emploi: This name appears only once in the Bible, in Nehemiah 11:9, where Judah son of Senua is named as the second leader of Jerusalem during the reconstruction period after the exile. It is an administrative document from the post-exilic times that lists the leaders and families who returned to Jerusalem. The context suggests that it was a family of notable Benjamites with some authority in managing the affairs of the city.

sens: Sudden loss of sight
Inability to see, to perceive
State of mental confusion or disorientation
H5575.detail:
1. It is the brutal deprivation of the ability to see: the eyes remain open but see no more. In Genesis 19:11, the angels strike the inhabitants of Sodom with blindness as they attempt to force the door of Lot's house — they tire themselves out searching for the entrance without being able to see it. 
2. More broadly, it is any state that prevents someone from seeing clearly: a physical or mental inability to discern reality. In 2 Kings 6:18, Elisha prays to the Lord to strike the Syrian soldiers surrounding him with blindness: they lose the ability to recognize the places and people around them. 
3. The word also refers to the disorientation of the mind, when one no longer understands what is happening: the Syrians, struck with blindness, no longer know where they are or toward whom they are walking.
H5575.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root meaning "to close" or "to obscure." It describes the image of eyelids or eyes closed to the light. The form used here is a plural that emphasizes the complete obscuring of both eyes. It is a sudden and particular affliction or punishment, not a simple weakness of sight.
H5575.emploi: The word appears only twice in the Hebrew Bible, always in contexts of miraculous divine judgment. In Genesis 19:11, God strikes the men of Sodom who threatened the angels. In 2 Kings 6:18, the prophet Elisha intercedes for the Lord to blind the Syrian enemies who were pursuing him. In both cases, it is a supernatural and temporary act: blindness is sent as a sign of God's power and as protection for His own.
H5575.portee: This blindness shows how God protects His people and His messengers. It is also a warning: unbelief and hostility toward God's messengers can attract judgment. For the believer, the word reminds us that God sees all our actions and has extraordinary means to accomplish His will — He is never without resources in the face of evil.

sens: King of Assyria who reigned from 705 to 681 B.C.
Son of King Sargon and father of Esarhaddon
The one who attacked the kingdom of Judah during the reign of Hezekiah
H5576.detail:
1. Sennacherib is the king of Assyria who, in the fourteenth year of Hezekiah's reign, invaded the kingdom of Judah and captured its fortified cities (2 Kings 18:13; 2 Chronicles 32:1). He was a powerful monarch who commanded a formidable army and sent his servants to intimidate Jerusalem by speaking against the living God (2 Chronicles 32:9; Isaiah 37:17).
2. He was the son of King Sargon and the father of King Esarhaddon, which shows that he belonged to the Assyrian royal dynasty and held a central place in the political history of the ancient Near East.
3. Divine intervention played a decisive role in the conflict: in response to Hezekiah's prayer, God sent an angel who killed 185,000 Assyrian soldiers, delivering Judah from the hand of Sennacherib and all his enemies (2 Chronicles 32:22).
H5576.origine: The name Sennacherib comes from the Akkadian Sennacherib, which means "Sin multiplied the brothers" (Sin being the moon god in Mesopotamian mythology). It is the historical name of the Assyrian king known from Assyrian archives and inscriptions from the 7th century B.C., and the Bible also refers to him by his other name, Sargon.
H5576.emploi: Sennacherib appears thirteen times in the biblical texts, mainly in Kings and Chronicles, and also in Isaiah. He is always presented as the king of Assyria who threatened Judah: he attacked the fortified cities (2 Kings 18:13), sent emissaries to intimidate Hezekiah and Jerusalem (2 Chronicles 32:9), and uttered insults against the God of Israel (Isaiah 37:17). His army was considerable, but God defeated it supernaturally, sealing his defeat and return home (2 Kings 19:36).
H5576.portee: The story of Sennacherib teaches the Christian reader that human powers, even the most impressive, can do nothing against God and His promise to His children. Faced with an apparently invincible enemy, Hezekiah turned to the Lord in prayer, and God acted to deliver His people. It is a testimony to the power and faithfulness of God toward those who seek Him.

sens: Branch of a tree, especially of the date palm
Stem that bears fruits or flowers
H5577.detail: 1. A branch is a division of the trunk or a large branch of a tree. The word here particularly refers to the branches of the date palm, the emblematic tree of the biblical Near East, on which dates grow. 2. More broadly, it is the part of the tree from which fruits or flowers hang — what the Bible also calls a "branch" that bears fruit. In the Song of Solomon, the beloved woman is compared to a palm tree whose branches can be grasped (Song of Solomon 7:9), an image of generous beauty and fertility.
H5577.origine: The Hebrew word sansinn literally refers to the branch or stem of the date palm. It is a concrete term, derived from the observation of this major tree in the land of Israel. The root evokes the very structure of the tree that divides into branches bearing fruit.
H5577.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Song of Solomon 7:9. It is used in a poetic and romantic context: the beloved envisions climbing the palm tree to grasp its branches, in an image of desire and intimacy. This passage compares the beloved woman herself to a palm tree, suggesting her slender beauty and fertility.
H5577.portee: This word reminds us that physical beauty and marital love are honored in Scripture. The palm tree, a noble and fruitful tree of the desert, symbolizes the beloved woman in all her grace. For the reader, it is an invitation to see love as a gift from God, worthy of wonder and poetry.

sens: City in the south of Judah
H5578.detail: Sansanna is a small city mentioned only once in Scripture, listed among the cities of the Negev (the desert south of Judah). It appears in Joshua 15:31, in the enumeration of cities assigned to the tribe of Judah during the division of the promised land. Its Hebrew name evokes a "branch of a palm tree," a poetic image that may suggest the vegetation or resources of the place.
H5578.origine: The name Sansanna comes from Hebrew and literally means "branch of a palm tree." This formation is based on a word for the leaf or branch of the palm tree, a characteristic tree of the ancient Near East. This type of name evokes either a particularity of the local landscape or a richness or beauty associated with this precious plant.
H5578.emploi: Sansanna appears only once in the Bible, in Joshua 15:31, where it is listed among the cities of the territory of Judah in the Negev region. It is included in an administrative list that reflects the borders and possessions of Judah after the conquest of Canaan. Its textual isolation suggests that it was a minor locality, although its place in this official list confirms its status as a fortified or established city in southern Judah.

sens: membrane ou appendice plat qui permet au poisson de se mouvoir et de se diriger dans l'eau
caractéristique distinctive qui détermine si un animal aquatique est pur ou impur selon la loi mosaïque
H5579.detail:
1. A fin is the part of a fish's body that allows it to swim and navigate in the water. It is an appendage or membrane that the fish moves to advance or turn. In the verses of Leviticus and Deuteronomy, fins are mentioned alongside scales as the two distinguishing signs of fish (Leviticus 11:9).
2. The presence of fins and scales determines the legal purity of an aquatic animal in Israel. Only animals that possess these two characteristics can be eaten; all those that lack them are considered impure and abominable (Leviticus 11:10 to 11:12). This is a practical and visible criterion for distinguishing what is permitted from what is forbidden at the Israelite table.
H5579.origine: The Hebrew word senappîr literally refers to what "divides" or "separates," with the fin being a part that clearly detaches from the fish's body. It is specific to the vocabulary of dietary purity laws in the Old Testament and appears only in legislative passages concerning permitted or forbidden food.
H5579.emploi: The word fin appears only five times in the Hebrew Bible, exclusively in the dietary codes of Leviticus and Deuteronomy. It is always associated with scales and specifically applies to aquatic creatures. In Leviticus 11:9 and Deuteronomy 14:9, fins are mentioned as a positive condition ("You may eat of all that have fins"), while in verses 11:10, 11:12, and 14:10, their absence renders the animal impure and forbidden. The term is purely descriptive and technical, used in a legislative context to establish clear and practical distinctions.
H5579.portee: For the believing reader, the term fin reminds us that God has established dietary purity laws based on visible and objective criteria, accessible to all Israelites. These prescriptions were not arbitrary: they were based on natural differences between clean and unclean creatures. Understanding that fins and scales precisely marked clean fish invites the believer to recognize God's wisdom in creation and in the distinction between what is lawful and what is not.

sens: Small insect that gnaws at fabrics
Slow and invisible destruction of what is precious
Biblical image of wear and fragility of human things
H5580.detail:
1. The moth is a small insect in its larval stage that burrows into wool or linen fabrics, gradually finding and gnawing at them until they are destroyed. In Isaiah 51:8, it symbolizes this inevitable destruction: it devours clothing as it silently eats away at the very substance of material things.
2. The word more broadly evokes hidden decomposition, that which wears away and destroys without noise or apparent violence. Unlike a fire that ravages everything in an instant, the moth represents a slow and inexorable ruin, impossible to stop once it has settled in.
3. In its only biblical usage (Isaiah 51:8), the moth stands in stark contrast to the justice and salvation of God that remain eternal: while humanity's garments are eaten away and turn to dust, divine faithfulness persists unchanged from age to age.
H5580.origine: The Hebrew word סָס (sas) literally refers to the moth, this destructive insect. Its primary image is that of the larva that gnaws, that which burrows and devastates from within. The word belongs to a very concrete register, rooted in the daily experience of the ancient Near East where insects ravaged stored fabrics. This sensory image — the silent gnawing — has naturally served as a biblical metaphor to express inevitable and progressive destruction.
H5580.emploi: The word moth appears only once in the Bible, in Isaiah 51:8. It is part of a prophetic passage where God comforts Israel by reminding them that oppressors will perish like garments eaten away by moths, while His salvation and justice are eternal. This unique usage makes it a highly symbolic word, used for its vivid imagery rather than for a precise entomological reference. The image chosen by the prophet Isaiah speaks directly to daily concerns: all material goods are subject to degradation.
H5580.portee: This word invites the Christian to reflect on the fragility of all that is earthly and perishable. In the face of external threats and the wear of time, trust must rest not on wealth or human power, but on the justice and salvation of God alone, which know no erosion. It is a call to detach one's heart from things that are eaten away to cling to what endures.

sens: Man of the tribe of Judah
H5581.detail: Sismaï is a character from the Old Testament belonging to the tribe of Judah, living during the time of the divided monarchy (around the 8th-6th century B.C.). He appears in the genealogy of Jerehmeel, an important clan of Judah. His Hebrew name evokes the image of a water crane or a swallow, symbols of lightness and movement. He is the son of Elasa and the father of Shallum (1 Chronicles 2:40).
H5581.origine: The name Sismaï comes from Hebrew and literally means "water crane" or "swallow," fast and graceful birds. It reflects a common practice among the Hebrews: giving children names evocative of animals or natural phenomena. Sismaï belongs to the lineage of Sheshan, an ancestor of the royal line of Judah, which underscores his genealogical importance in the history of Israel.
H5581.emploi: Sismaï appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 2:40, where he is listed in the detailed genealogy of the tribe of Judah, particularly in the line of Jerehmeel. The Bible mentions him simply as a link in a genealogical chain: he is the son of Elasa and the father of Shallum. His inclusion in these lists shows that the Bible values family transmission and generational heritage, even for minor characters.

sens: To provide someone with food or physical strength
To strengthen or fortify the heart, soul, spirit
To uphold, support, or hold someone in difficulty
To confirm, establish, or strengthen an institution, power
H5582.detail:
1. To support someone by nourishing them or giving them physical strength: this is to meet their material needs to keep them alive and healthy. In Genesis 18:5, Abraham offers a piece of bread to "strengthen" the hearts of his guests; in Psalms 104:15, bread "supports" the heart of man as essential food.
2. To strengthen or encourage someone morally and spiritually, particularly their heart: this is to give courage, confidence, or consolation. In Judges 19:8, someone is invited to "strengthen" their heart before departing; in Psalms 41:4, the Lord "supports" the sick on their bed by comforting them.
3. To uphold someone in danger or weakness, to prop them up: this is to hold them firm in the face of trials. In Psalms 18:36, God's hand "supports" the one who fights; in Psalms 94:18, when the foot slips, it is the Lord's help that "supports".
4. To affirm, confirm, or establish a power, a throne, an institution: this is to keep them stable and enduring. In Proverbs 20:28, the king "supports" his throne by kindness; this word then designates the action of consolidating and securing it.
H5582.origine: Hebrew root קְנָה (qanah), from the simple image of holding, carrying, supporting. The word belongs to a common Semitic family: Aramaic has the same verb in the form סְעַד (seʿad). The fundamental idea is that of a support, a backing given to something or someone to prevent them from falling or bending.
H5582.emploi: This verb appears 12 times in the Old Testament, mainly in the Psalms and the book of Kings, but also in the heart of Genesis and in Proverbs. It primarily describes material help: feeding someone (Genesis 18:5, Judges 19:8). However, the Bible uses it more in the sense of moral and spiritual support, particularly the action of God who strengthens a failing heart (Psalms 41:4) or who holds back the slipping foot (Psalms 94:18). It also characterizes divine support for the fighter (Psalms 18:36) or for the king who establishes his authority (Proverbs 20:28, Isaiah 9:6). The word thus glides from the concrete (the bread that nourishes) to the spiritual (the grace that comforts).
H5582.portee: This word reveals how the Lord does not abandon us in our weaknesses. He "supports" us when we stumble, nourishes and comforts us, and gives us the courage to continue. For the believer, this means that God is a reliable and constant support, always at hand in trials, and that our strength comes from Him, not from ourselves.

sens: To support someone in their efforts or work
To actively help, by staying with someone
H5583.detail:
1. This verb evokes the idea of supporting someone by helping them accomplish a task. In Ezra 5:2, the prophets of God "assisted" Zerubbabel and Joshua in the reconstruction of the temple: they were by their side to encourage and help them in this great undertaking. It is an active and present support.
2. More broadly, "to assist" means to be present to help, to support someone in carrying out their mission or work. It is not a passive or distant help, but a presence that accompanies and strengthens.
H5583.origine: This Aramaic word comes from the same root as the Hebrew verb "saaad" (סָעַד), which also means "to support" or "to help." The basic image is that of giving support, serving as a point of support for someone. The form used here (Aphel in Aramaic) indicates a causative action: to make support, to make help.
H5583.emploi: This verb appears only once in the Bible, in Ezra 5:2, in the context of the return from exile and the reconstruction of the temple after the Babylonian captivity. The prophets Haggai and Zechariah "assisted" the leaders of the project by encouraging and supporting them. The word emphasizes the essential role of the prophets who not only spoke but actively accompanied the people in this spiritual and material restoration. This unique usage shows how prophetic support was indispensable to the success of God's work.
H5583.portee: This word reminds us that serving God is never a solitary affair. Even great leaders like Zerubbabel and Joshua needed to be assisted, encouraged, and supported by the prophets. It invites the Christian to seek and offer mutual support in fulfilling God's mission: the Church is built only through the constant fraternal support of one another.

sens: to move with speed and force, as if carried by an external power
to act with impetuous haste, without restraint
H5584.detail:
1. The word primarily evokes the violent and rapid movement of a natural force that sweeps everything in its path. In Psalm 55:9, it is the storm wind that "rushes": the psalmist wishes to flee "faster than the impetuous wind," in other words, as quickly as a gust that cannot be restrained. The image is one of something that charges irresistibly.
2. Figuratively, the verb applies to human action: to rush means to act with feverish haste, driven by an urgency or passion that cannot wait. It conveys the idea of being swept away by an inner force, just as the wind carries leaves.
H5584.origine: The Hebrew verb סָעָה comes from a root that expresses violent and rapid movement. Its primary meaning is associated with meteorological phenomena (wind, storm) that symbolize an uncontrollable power. The root carries the idea of an action that exceeds the normal, that overflows and carries away.
H5584.emploi: The verb appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Psalm 55:9. It is a rare term, reserved for an intense poetic context. The author of the psalm, faced with the betrayal of a friend, expresses his desire to flee with extreme speed, that of a storm wind. The choice of this rare and dynamic word enhances the emotion of the passage: the psalmist's haste is not a mere ordinary rush; it is an almost superhuman flight, driven by despair and indignation.
H5584.portee: This word teaches that haste can be legitimate in the face of a real threat, and that the Bible acknowledges the urgency of serious circumstances. It also reminds us that our strong emotions — fear, indignation, the desire to escape an intolerable situation — find their expression in prayer, where the psalmist does not suppress them but entrusts them to God by naming them with intensity.

sens: opening or hollow in a rock, where one can hide
narrow crevice in stone or rock
branch or twig of a tree
H5585.detail:
1. The primary meaning is a natural cavity in the rock, large enough for a person to take refuge. It is this hollow or opening that offers protection and shelter. Samson "withdrew into the cave of the rock of Etam" (Judges 15:8) after defeating the Philistines: he hides in this rocky refuge.
2. The word also designates a simple fissure, a narrow crack that opens in the stone. During God's judgment, men "will enter the clefts of the rocks" (Isaiah 2:21) to find shelter: the crevice becomes a last resort refuge.
3. By extension, the word applies to branches and twigs of a tree, which also form hollows and divisions. "Four, five [olives], in its fruiting branches" (Isaiah 17:6): it refers to the natural division of wood that branches out.
H5585.origine: This Hebrew word comes from a root that expresses the idea of dividing or splitting. A cave is a place where the rock has opened or split; a branch is where the trunk divides. The common image is one of separation, a division that creates an opening or branching.
H5585.emploi: The word appears six times in the Bible, always in the Old Testament. In Judges 15 (two occurrences), it literally refers to the cave of the rock of Etam, a natural refuge. In Isaiah 2:21 and 57:5, it evokes the clefts of the rocks, contexts of dread and judgment. Isaiah 17:6 and 27:10 apply it to the branches of trees (olive, bush). The word thus oscillates between two images: the protective opening and the natural division of the living.
H5585.portee: This word reminds us that God knows all the refuges where man believes he can hide, even the most secret ones: the clefts of the rocks will not suffice to shelter him from divine judgment. It also speaks of fragility: like an isolated branch on a shaken tree, the remnant of the people will be few. It is an invitation not to seek in vain for earthly shelters, but to turn to God alone.

sens: to cut or break the branches of a tree violently
to strip, to fell (in a figurative sense)
H5586.detail:
1. The word denotes the action of breaking or cutting the branches of a tree, particularly in a sudden and violent manner. The image is one of a force that breaks the twigs: in Isaiah 10:33, the Lord "breaks" the branches violently, cutting them from the great trees.
2. Figuratively, the word evokes the downfall, the destruction of a power or greatness — the idea that only the branches are cut suggests a selective spoliation or the humiliation of what rises high.
H5586.origine: The Hebrew verb סָעַף comes from a root that evokes the idea of cutting or breaking. The form used here is the Piel, which intensifies the action: it is not simply to cut, but to "break well," "break with force." The primary image is that of a blade or force that penetrates the wood, as one trims a hedge or prunes a tree.
H5586.emploi: This verb appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Isaiah 10:33. It is used in a judgment oracle where the Lord, like a powerful lumberjack, mutilates the majestic trees of the forest. This context of forest imagery and the downfall of a superb greatness gives the word its tone of irreversible destruction and dispossession.
H5586.portee: This term reminds us that apparent power — that of the great trees that stand tall — is nothing before the hand of the Lord. For the reader, the image of the divine lumberjack invites us not to place our trust in what rises and boasts, but in God alone, who brings down pride with the same certainty as one breaks a branch.

sens: lateral position, flank of a person or thing
opposite direction, opposing party or camp
hesitation between two positions, inner division
H5587A.detail:
1. The primary meaning designates the physical side of a person or object — its flank, what is to the left or right. However, the Bible rarely uses this word in this purely material sense.
2. The word takes on new force when it speaks of opposing positions, enemy camps, or rival parties. It conveys the idea of a rupture, a separation between two contrary directions.
3. In 1 Kings 18:21, Elijah says to the people: "How long will you waver between two sides?" — that is, how long will you remain divided, oscillating between God and Baal without choosing? The word here evokes ambivalence, indecision that tears the soul, the refusal to decisively choose one side or the other.
H5587A.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that denotes the idea of bending, leaning — hence the image of a side position, or a flexion. Literally, "to waver between two sides" means to lean alternately from one side to the other, like a scale that never stops. The image is one of physical hesitation that manifests moral indecision.
H5587A.emploi: This word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in 1 Kings 18:21. Elijah uses it to reproach the people of Israel for their lack of decision in the face of the fundamental religious issue: to serve the true God or to follow false gods. The context makes it a word loaded with spiritual meaning — not merely a physical position, but a state of soul, a moral division of those who refuse to fully commit.
H5587A.portee: This word speaks to the Christian about the demand for clarity and choice in faith. Jesus will echo this demand when he says that one cannot serve two masters. The text invites us to examine our own inner divisions — these "sides" between which we waver — and to recognize them for what they are: unfaithfulness. True conversion involves abandoning this oscillation.

sens: Moment où l'esprit est troublé
Pensées qui surgissent avec force et urgence
État d'inquiétude ou de perturbation intérieure
H5587B.detail:
1. The word first designates the precise moment when the spirit is shaken, as when night visions disturb the mind during sleep (Job 4:13). It is the instant when something comes to disrupt inner calm.
2. It also expresses thoughts that force someone to react, which rise within them with a certain violence. Elihu says that his thoughts compel him to respond, so pressing are they (Job 20:2): they cannot remain contained.
3. More broadly, the word paints an agitated inner state, a disturbance of the heart or spirit, like an internal swell that pushes toward action or speech.
H5587B.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that evokes the idea of moving, shaking, agitating. It designates what troubles, what disturbs the tranquility of the mind. It is a physical image — that of movement, of agitation — applied to the inside: thoughts that press and shake the soul like the wind shakes the trees.
H5587B.emploi: The word appears twice in the book of Job, in two closely related contexts. First, it depicts the moment when night visions disturb thought during deep sleep (Job 4:13): it is the critical instant when calm is broken. Then, it describes the inner urgency that compels Elihu to speak (Job 20:2): his thoughts grip him so tightly that he cannot remain silent. In both cases, the word expresses a force that comes from within and deprives one of rest or silence.
H5587B.portee: This word helps us recognize the biblical experience of inner agitation — that which can be caused by visions of God, urgent thoughts, intuitions that arise. It shows that a forced word can be the sign of a real inner pressure, not always negative: it can also be that of a conviction that cannot remain silent.

sens: qui est divisé, qui va dans deux directions à la fois
qui manque de sincérité ou de conviction
qui hésite ou se dérobe
H5588.detail: 1. The word literally designates what is divided or split, like something cleaved into two parts — a separation that prevents unity. 2. Figuratively, it describes a divided heart or soul, someone who does not fully commit: "I hate those who are divided, but I love your law" (Psalms 119:113). 3. It is the attitude of one who wants to serve two masters at once, who loves God with one hand and the world with the other, without true sincerity.
H5588.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that evokes division or separation. It expresses the idea of something that stands on the edge, that has not taken a side, that refuses to choose completely. It is the opposite of totality and the whole-hearted commitment of the heart.
H5588.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Psalm 119:113. In this context, the psalmist expresses his hatred for the "divided" men — those whose piety is superficial or inconsistent, who only partially attach themselves to God. It is a rare word that underscores the importance for the believer of total adherence to God, without compromise.
H5588.portee: This term challenges the reader regarding the integrity of their faith: have we truly given our hearts to God, or do we remain divided between Him and our interests? It is an invitation to spiritual authenticity and a rejection of half-measures.

sens: Ramification d'un tronc d'arbre
Partie d'un arbre où se posent les oiseaux et où pousse le feuillage
H5589.detail:
1. A branch is each of the main or secondary ramifications that come from the trunk of a tree. The word evokes the living structure of the tree, its divisions that allow the plant to extend toward the sky. In Ezekiel 31:8, the prophet speaks of the majestic branches of a great tree, comparing their grandeur to that of the cedars and cypresses of God's garden.

2. The branches are also the place where birds nest and where animals find shelter. It is on the branches that creatures find refuge and food, making it an essential element of the tree's life. In Ezekiel 31:6, the vision of a tree whose branches shelter all the birds of the sky and all the beasts of the fields symbolizes a power that protects and sustains entire peoples.
H5589.origine: The Hebrew word *se'appah* specifically designates the ramification of living wood. It comes from a root that evokes the idea of dividing, of extending. In the Old Testament, the word is found only twice, both in Ezekiel 31, in a poetic and symbolic description. The context of these uses shows that it is a prophetic word aimed at representing ancient Egypt as a dominant tree: the branches become the image of its power extending protection and shade over other nations.
H5589.emploi: The word appears only twice in the Hebrew Bible, exclusively in Ezekiel 31. This passage is a prophetic allegory where a great tree symbolizes greatness and dominance. In Ezekiel 31:6, the branches shelter the birds and beasts, illustrating the protective power of the tree. In Ezekiel 31:8, the branches are described as rivaling in beauty with the branches of the greatest trees in God's garden. These two occurrences show that the word is used in a context of majesty and grandiloquent comparison.
H5589.portee: This image of branches that shelter all living beings invites the Christian to meditate on divine protection. The majestic tree that Ezekiel spoke of evokes the promise of a safe shelter and shade for those who trust in God. However, the context of the passage also reminds us that earthly power, no matter how great, is never comparable to that of the divine Creator.

sens: S'agiter violemment, en parlant du vent ou d'une tempête
Être agité, secoué, malmené par les éléments ou les circonstances
Être rempli de fureur ou de colère intense
H5590.detail: 1. The most concrete meaning is that of a storm that unleashes, of a violent wind that blows with force. In Isaiah 54:11, the city is "beaten by the storm," a poetic image of a person tormented by misfortunes. 2. The word also describes the state of a person or thing that undergoes this violence: agitated, shaken, battered. In Hosea 13:3, the grain is "carried away by the wind" out of the threshing floor, and in Jonah 1:11-13, the sea becomes "stormy" and grows "more and more" agitated against the sailors. 3. The word also applies to inner fury, the rage of the heart. In 2 Kings 6:11, the king of Syria has a heart that is "agitated" when he discovers the unfaithfulness of his servants: his heart rages like a storm.
H5590.origine: The Hebrew verb סָעַר comes from a root that evokes violent and tumultuous movement. The basic image is that of wind or storm that stirs and sweeps everything in its path. This word belongs to the family of Hebrew words describing fury and agitation: it can express both the unleashing of nature and that of human emotions or divine anger.
H5590.emploi: This verb appears 7 times in the Old Testament. It is first used to describe unleashed elements: the wind that tears, the storm at sea (Jonah 1:11-13, Habakkuk 3:14). It also designates the physical and moral agitation of a person struck by misfortune (Isaiah 54:11, Hosea 13:3). Finally, it expresses the outburst of the heart, inner fury, as in 2 Kings 6:11 where the king feels troubled and enraged. The word can also be used to describe an aggressive action, a rush (Habakkuk 3:14: the enemies rush "like the storm").
H5590.portee: This word invites the reader to recognize that the storms of life — trials, injustices, terrors — have a reality and a force, but they are never outside of God's control. Isaiah 54:11 shows it: even the city "beaten by the storm" is not abandoned; God promises it magnificent restoration. For the Christian, this word reminds that their own inner storms (fury, turmoil) can be calmed by trusting in the one who commands the wind and the sea.

sens: Violent atmospheric disturbance with very strong wind
Manifestation of God's anger, divine judgment
H5591A.detail:
1. A storm is a violent disturbance of the sky where the wind blows with destructive power. It is the concrete meteorological phenomenon: a thunderstorm, a violent gust. In Jonah 1:4, "the Lord sent a great wind upon the sea, and there arose a mighty storm," we see this material sense — a real storm that threatens the boat.
2. The storm becomes the image of God's anger in action. When Jeremiah says, "Behold, the storm of the Lord, the fury breaks out" (Jeremiah 23:19), the storm is not just a natural phenomenon: it symbolizes God's judgment that falls upon the wicked. It is the visible manifestation of His wrathful justice.
H5591A.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that expresses agitation, collapse, chaos. The storm naturally evokes the idea of confusion and destruction: everything is shaken, overturned. The same root is found in other words expressing tumult and agitation. As a destructive force, the storm becomes in the Bible a favored image of divine power, of judgment that shakes everything in its path.
H5591A.emploi: The word appears 8 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in the prophetic books (Jeremiah) and the Psalms. In the Psalms, it is first a real storm that threatens (Psalms 55:9) or that the psalmist asks God to unleash upon his enemies (Psalms 83:16). But in the prophets, particularly Jeremiah, the storm almost systematically becomes a metaphor for divine judgment: in Jeremiah 23:19 and 30:23 (the same formula), the storm of the Lord falls upon the wicked. It represents both God's raw power and His wrathful intervention in history.
H5591A.portee: Understanding that the storm is for the Bible an image of God's judgment helps the reader grasp how Scripture speaks of divine justice: not in an abstract way, but through images that strike the imagination — violence, inevitability, irresistible force. For those who fear God, it is a warning. For the reader of Jonah, it is also a reminder that even the elements obey God: the storm is never an accident, it is sent.

sens: Violent meteorological phenomenon: wind, rain, storm that unleash with force
Whirling movement of air that carries things away in its path
Manifestation of God's power and anger
Divine judgment against the wicked
H5591B.detail:
1. A storm is primarily a violent natural phenomenon: a thunderstorm with powerful winds that lift the waves of the sea (Psalms 107:25) or that carries away like chaff (Isaiah 40:24). It is the raw force of unleashed nature.
2. The word also evokes the whirlwind, this swirling movement that carries everything in its path: Elijah is taken up to heaven in a whirlwind (2 Kings 2:1), a spectacular image of a force that takes away.
3. In the Bible, the storm is never neutral: it manifests the power of God Himself. God "speaks, and He makes the storm blow" (Psalms 107:25), showing that nature obeys His voice.
4. The storm also becomes the symbol of divine judgment: "Behold, the storm of the Lord, the fury breaks out" (Jeremiah 23:19), it falls upon the heads of the wicked as an expression of His anger.
H5591B.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that designates tumult, violent noise, agitation. It is from the same family as "sa.ar" (סַעַר), the masculine form that also means storm or tempest. The central idea is that of a power that stirs, that moves violently, either literally or metaphorically.
H5591B.emploi: This word appears 16 times in the Old Testament, mainly in the poetic and prophetic books. It first refers to real storms: God calms the storm on the sea (Psalms 107:25-29), or it destroys plants (Isaiah 40:24). But it is also used for divine revelations: God speaks to Job out of the storm (Job 38:1), marking the importance and solemnity of His word. Finally, it represents God's judgment: in Jeremiah and Ezekiel, the Lord's storm comes to strike the wicked (Jeremiah 23:19, Ezekiel 13:11-13), it is the weapon of His justice.
H5591B.portee: For the believer, the storm reminds us that God controls the forces of the world and that no natural power escapes His control. It also teaches that God often speaks to the heart amid agitation and confusion, not in spite of it. But it also warns: God's storm is real, and His justice is executed against those who reject Him.

sens: Shallow container designed to hold a liquid
Cup or small goblet
Figuratively, situation or destiny poured out upon a people
H5592A.detail:
1. The basin is a wide and shallow container, made of various materials (gold, silver, clay), used to collect or pour a liquid. At Passover, the basin holds the blood of the lamb that is applied to the doorposts with a branch of hyssop (Exodus 12:22). It is a practical and common utensil.
2. The cup is a smaller, more tapered container, intended for drinking or serving beverages, as well as an ornamental object used in the Temple worship (1 Kings 7:50). In these contexts, it is often a precious object, made of gold or silver.
3. Figuratively, the word can refer to destiny or judgment poured out like a drink: "I will make Jerusalem a cup of staggering" (Zechariah 12:2) means that the city will undergo the shock and confusion of divine judgment, like someone drinking an intoxicating beverage.
H5592A.origine: The Hebrew word saph comes from a root that evokes the idea of pouring or extending. It is a concrete term designating a hollow and open object, shallow, capable of receiving or containing. The word belongs to the family of service and kitchen utensils, very common in ancient daily life.
H5592A.emploi: The word saph appears 6 times in the Old Testament, mainly in passages describing worship and the Temple. It first refers to the basins used at Passover (Exodus 12:22) or the basins and cups that adorned the Temple of Jerusalem and its altars (1 Kings 7:50; 2 Kings 12:13; Jeremiah 52:19). In these contexts, it is a ritual or liturgical object of great importance. Once, in Zechariah 12:2, the word takes on a figurative sense to denote divine judgment poured out upon a people, a powerful image of misfortune that falls like a drink one is forced to consume.
H5592A.portee: This word reminds the reader of the practical detail of salvation: the blood of the lamb poured into a basin and applied to the lintel of the door saves the firstborn of Israel. It is a concrete act, a simple gesture of faith, that seals the covenant between God and His people. For the Christian, this foreshadows the blood of Jesus poured out for salvation. The word also shows how God cares about everyday objects and the worship of the Temple, thus sanctifying ordinary life.

sens: The frame or bar that marks the entrance of a door or building
The stone or wood strip placed at the bottom of an opening
The one who guards the entrance, the doorkeeper
H5592B.detail:
1. The threshold is the frame or bar that forms the lower limit of a door. It is the structural element that one crosses when entering a house or building. In Ezekiel 40:6, the prophet precisely measures the thresholds of the temple doors: this stone concretely marked the passage from one space to another.
2. The threshold can refer to the step or stone strip at the bottom of an entrance. When the Levite's wife is found dead in Judges 19:27, she lies "at the entrance of the house, her hands on the threshold" — it is this physical surface that she touches in dying.
3. By extension, the threshold refers to the one who guards this entrance, the doorkeeper. At the temple gates, the guardians of the thresholds (1 Chronicles 9:19) were Levites responsible for monitoring. In Esther 6:2, Bigthan and Teresh, "guards of the threshold," are the eunuchs who controlled access to the king.
H5592B.origine: The Hebrew word saph comes from a root that evokes the idea of stripping or sweeping — hence probably the image of the threshold as a surface on which one places their foot. In the Hebrew Bible, the same word describes both the part of the building (the physical threshold) and the function of the one who guards it (the doorkeeper or guardian). This extension of meaning is natural: the guardian of the threshold is the one who stands there, at the heart of this passage.
H5592B.emploi: The word "threshold" appears about twenty times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in narratives or architectural descriptions. It is often found in texts related to the temple: the Levites guarded the thresholds (1 Chronicles 9:19, 2 Chronicles 23:4), and the money collected for the temple was given to "those who had charge of the threshold" (2 Kings 22:4). Ezekiel, meticulously describing the future temple, measures the thresholds of the doors (Ezekiel 40:6, 40:7). The word also appears in historical contexts: the guards of the threshold of the king in Esther (Esther 6:2), or priests massacred at the thresholds of the temple (2 Kings 25:18). The meaning remains constant: the physical limit of the entrance, or the one who stands guard there.
H5592B.portee: The threshold is a biblical symbol of passage and separation — between outside and inside, between the profane and the sacred. Standing at the threshold of the temple means being at the heart of the encounter with God. For the Christian, this image of crossing the threshold reminds us that accessing the presence of God requires a passage, a decision, and vigilance on the part of those who guard the entrance of His people. It is a simple word that anchors faith in reality: God is encountered in a specific place, with guardians, rules, and architecture.

sens: One of the sons of the giant Rapha, a Philistine warrior from the time of the united monarchy in Israel
H5593.detail: Saph was one of the sons of the giant Rapha, a family of formidable Philistine warriors. He is mentioned only once in the Bible, during a battle between Israel and the Philistines in the time of King David, where the Israelite warrior Sibbecai the Hushathite killed him (2 Samuel 21:18). His name means "great" or "exalted," which is fitting for a man of the race of giants. He was the brother of Goliath, the famous giant defeated by David, which shows that the threat of the Philistine giants persisted long after Goliath's death.
H5593.origine: The name Saph literally means "great" or "exalted" in Hebrew, an appropriate image for a tall warrior. He is also known as Sippai (סִפַּי) in the parallel account in 1 Chronicles 20:4. This warrior belongs to the lineage of Rapha, a renowned family of Philistine giants who regularly threatened Israel.
H5593.emploi: Saph appears only once in the Bible, in 2 Samuel 21:18, during a series of battles between Israel and the Philistines in the time of King David. This passage recounts how Sibbecai the Hushathite killed him during a battle at Gob. The same incident is reported in 1 Chronicles 20:4, where he is called Sippai. These two accounts emphasize that long after Goliath's death, the threat of the Philistine giants continued to weigh on Israel, and that God regularly granted His warriors victory over these formidable adversaries.

sens: To express sorrow and pain by shedding tears and crying
To mourn, that is, to manifest grief at someone's death
To lament, to moan in regret or suffering
To be the object of others' weeping and lamentation
H5594.detail:
1. The word primarily denotes the act of weeping, shedding tears and crying out in response to pain or sorrow. It is a spontaneous and visible expression of suffering. In Ecclesiastes 12:7, we see "mourners" walking the streets: these are people whose profession is to weep publicly.
2. In a funeral context, "to weep" means to mourn: to honor the dead by the official and communal manifestation of grief. When Abraham comes to "weep" for Sarah (Genesis 23:2), he expresses his sorrow but also his respect for her. It is a solemn act, often accompanied by fasting and ceremony.
3. The word also describes lamentation, a cry of complaint mixed with regret or reproach. In Jeremiah 16:5, the Lord forbids the prophet from entering a house of mourning to "weep" and "lament": it is about audibly expressing one's affliction.
4. Sometimes, the word takes on a passive meaning: to be wept for, to be the object of others' lamentation (Jeremiah 34:5: "they will weep for you"). This is thus to receive honor and respect after death.
H5594.origine: The Hebrew root saphadh evokes the image of cries and tears shed in public, a noisy manifestation of pain. The word belongs to the family of expressions of mourning and sorrow in Hebrew. It has no known distant etymology, but it is attested in other Semitic languages with similar meanings. It is a term fundamentally linked to the mourning customs of the ancient Near East, where weeping for the dead was an important social rite.
H5594.emploi: The verb "to weep" (saphadh) appears 29 times in the Hebrew Bible, especially in historical narratives (Samuel, Kings) and among the prophets (Jeremiah, Ezekiel, Zechariah). It is very often used at the death of important figures: Abraham weeps for Sarah, people weep for King Josiah, people weep for the prophets (Jeremiah 16:4-6). The word can also describe lamentation over misfortunes: in Jeremiah 4:8, weeping expresses mourning in the face of judgment. In Ecclesiastes 3:4, weeping is the opposite of laughter, just as mourning is the opposite of joy. Finally, in Zechariah (12:10-12), weeping takes on a spiritual and messianic dimension: the nations will weep for the one they have pierced, an image of collective repentance.
H5594.portee: This word reminds us that in the biblical vision, expressing pain and sorrow is natural and honorable, not shameful. The tears shed for the dead acknowledge their dignity and testify to the human bond. For the believer, weeping is legitimate in the face of loss; Jesus Himself wept (John 11:35). But the Bible also anchors mourning within limits: it is a time of suffering that should not stifle trust in God. Finally, the eschatological vision of Zechariah transforms mourning into repentance: weeping can become the first step toward returning to God.

sens: To be taken away, torn away, forcibly removed
To be annihilated, destroyed, eliminated
To disappear, vanish
To be seized, captured, caught
To accumulate, add to something
H5595.detail:
1. The concrete and primary meaning is to be taken away or torn away. When one is seized, one is removed from where one was, taken away against one's will. It conveys the idea of suddenly disappearing from a place by an external force: "Escape to the mountain, lest you perish" (Genesis 19:17) means "flee or you will be taken away." 
2. The meaning broadens to destruction or annihilation: to perish is to be destroyed, to cease to exist. Abraham asks: "Will you also destroy the righteous with the wicked?" (Genesis 18:23), meaning to kill them, to annihilate them.
3. In certain contexts, perish simply describes the disappearance or end of something. It can mean that something ceases to be visible, available, or useful.
4. The word can also express the idea of being seized or captured: to be taken, caught by someone or something. "All who are taken will fall by the sword" (Isaiah 13:15): those who will be caught, taken.
5. In a different context, the verb means to accumulate or add to: "I will add drunkenness to thirst" (Deuteronomy 29:19) shows how the same verb can denote the act of accumulating, piling one thing on another.
H5595.origine: The Hebrew verb סָפָה comes from a root that evokes sweeping, a broom (סָפַר may have a distant connection to the idea of stripping away, removing). The primary image is that of a broom sweeping away dust, removing, making disappear. From this comes the broader idea: to take away, to carry off, to annihilate. The word belongs to a Hebrew family that revolves around tearing away and elimination.
H5595.emploi: This verb appears 19 times in the Old Testament, mostly in historical narratives and prophetic warnings. In Genesis (Sodom), it denotes imminent destruction: God threatens to perish the righteous with the wicked, or Lot must flee lest he perish. In 1 Samuel, the warlike or judicial context emphasizes the meaning of "being killed" or "disappearing": David must flee for fear that Saul will make him perish. The Psalms use it to express the desire that the enemies of the righteous be removed from this world. Isaiah uses it to announce that all who are seized by the sword will perish. A notable exception is in Deuteronomy 29:19, where adding drunkenness to thirst shows that the same verb can mean "to pile up" or "to accumulate" in a less violent register.
H5595.portee: This word invites the reader to meditate on the reality and gravity of divine judgment. To perish is not an abstraction: it is to be taken away from the world, to cease to exist. For the Christian, this reminds us that sin has real and definitive consequences, and that God, in His justice, does not leave unpunished acts contrary to His covenant. It is also an exhortation to flee from evil and seek salvation, as Lot fled Sodom.

sens: To physically attach, unite two things together
To add oneself to a group, to join
To pour a liquid, to make it flow from a container
To push away, to remove someone from something
H5596A.detail:
1. The primary meaning is to attach, to bring two things together so that they hold together: in Isaiah 14:1, the strangers "will join to the house of Jacob" means they will incorporate into the people of Jacob, joining them in a lasting way.
2. In a group or community relationship, to join means to become a member, to connect: this is the meaning of the verb when talking about incorporating into a house or a nation.
3. The word can also refer to the action of pouring a liquid: in Habakkuk 2:15, "pouring out his wineskin" means to make the contents of a wineskin flow, to overflow from the container.
4. By extension, to join someone to a place or situation means to attach them there, and thus to push someone away from something means to detach them: in 1 Samuel 26:19, David says that his enemies "detach him from the inheritance of the Lord," meaning they chase him away from the land and the people of God.
H5596A.origine: The Hebrew verb סָפַח (saphach) evokes the image of joining, putting together. The root expresses the bringing together and union of two elements. It also appears in contexts where one pushes away or removes, as the opposite of the action of uniting: thus detaching someone means separating them, driving them away from the group or the land.
H5596A.emploi: The verb saphach appears five times in the Hebrew Bible, always with nuances related to union or separation. In Isaiah 14:1, it describes the strangers who unite with the restored people of Israel. In 1 Samuel 26:19, David uses the word detach to describe how they want to chase him from the promised land and communion with God. In Habakkuk 2:15, pouring means making the wine flow to intoxicate the next person. The context changes, but the idea of joining or separating remains constant.
H5596A.portee: This word reminds us of the importance of attachment: to God, to His people, to His inheritance. Being detached from the Lord is a painful separation. Conversely, joining the people of God is a beneficial union. David fears being chased away from the divine presence and his people; the strangers who join Israel find a place in the family of God. It is a powerful image of communion.

sens: To strike with baldness, to lose hair
To strip of one's natural ornament, to reduce to nakedness
H5596B.detail:
1. The word describes the action of striking someone with baldness, meaning to make them lose their hair. It is a physical affliction that affects the body: in Isaiah 3:17, the prophet announces that the Lord will make the top of the heads of the daughters of Zion bald — a promise of judgment that strikes with its strangeness and severity.
2. Beyond the literal sense, the word expresses the idea of stripping someone of what adorns or protects them, reducing them to shame and nakedness. Baldness here is a sign of dishonor and destruction: it removes beauty and respectable appearance. This biblical image conveys how God's judgment strips and humiliates the proud.
H5596B.origine: The word comes from a root that evokes the idea of striking or wounding. The form used here (Piel) emphasizes the action of causing or producing this effect: to make bald, to strike with baldness. It is a verb of direct action, describing a blow or affliction inflicted by God.
H5596B.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Isaiah 3:17. The prophet Isaiah announces God's judgment on the daughters of Zion (the women of Jerusalem) because of their pride and vanities. Making bald is presented as a concrete and humiliating punishment: the loss of hair symbolizes the loss of beauty, dignity, and honor. It is a strong image to express the reversal and shame that await the proud.
H5596B.portee: This word reminds us that God's judgment touches the heart of what honors us in the eyes of the world — our appearance, our status, our pride. It calls for vigilance against pride and self-love, and shows that true beauty and true dignity come from God, not from the adornments of the body.

sens: Skin eruption or inflammation
Skin lesion suspected of leprosy
Skin condition, benign or malignant
H5597.detail:
1. A dartre is a visible eruption or inflammation on the skin, a skin disease that the priest must examine (Leviticus 13:2). It is a spot or tumor that appears on the surface of the body and may resemble a leprous sore.
