2. In the system of the Law, the dartre is among the marks that may indicate ritual impurity: it must be verified by the priest to determine whether the person has leprosy or simply a benign condition (Leviticus 14:56). The term encompasses various skin lesions, whether serious or mild.
H5597.origine: The Hebrew word sappachat comes from a root that likely means "to flow" or "to spread," evoking the idea of something that emerges or extends over the skin. In biblical Hebrew, this word belongs to the family of terms describing skin diseases and ritual impurities. It is a term specific to the Levitical system of purity and impurity.
H5597.emploi: The word appears twice in Leviticus, at the heart of the Levitical purity code. In Leviticus 13:2, it refers to a skin eruption that must be examined by the priest to confirm or exclude leprosy. In Leviticus 14:56, the dartre is listed among the various skin conditions to which the rules of purity and impurity apply. In both cases, the context is medical and ritual: it is about determining the purity or impurity of the person before God.
H5597.portee: This term reminds us that in the Old Testament, illness is not only a physical matter but also a ritual and spiritual one. The careful examination of the dartre by the priest symbolizes the need for discernment in the life of God's people: knowing how to distinguish the serious from the benign, the impure from the pure. For the modern reader, this invites meditation on spiritual purification, a theme that Jesus transforms by calling for the conversion of the heart rather than mere external observance.

sens: Large Philistine warrior, son of Rapha
H5598.detail: Sippaï is a Philistine warrior from the family of giants, son of Rapha. He is killed by Sibbecai the Hushathite during a battle at Gezer (1 Chronicles 20:4). He appears as one of the brothers of Goliath and the other giants that David's warriors fought.
H5598.origine: The name Sippaï means "threshold" or "passage." It is a variant of another name, Saph, which refers to the same warrior. Both forms of the name are found in the parallel accounts of David's victories over the Philistine giants.
H5598.emploi: Sippaï is mentioned only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 20:4, where he is presented as one of the sons of Rapha and brother of Goliath. He is part of this dynasty of Philistine giants that David's mighty men fought during the wars against the Philistines. The Chronicle names him Sippaï, while 2 Samuel 21:18 calls him Saph.

sens: flow of water that flows forcefully
continuous flow that carries everything in its path
destructive power of what flows
H5599A.detail:
1. The word specifically refers to the current, that is, the water that flows forcefully from one place to another. In Job 14:19, the current of water crushes the stone: it is the image of a powerful and relentless flow.
2. By extension, it refers to the continuous and irresistible flow, one that carries and transforms everything in its path — here, the very earth is swept away by this current.
3. The word also evokes the hidden destructive power in this movement: flowing waters never cease, they wear away the hardest stone and carry off the most fertile soil, an image of insensible forces that slowly but surely destroy human hope.
H5599A.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that expresses the idea of flow, of that which flows or gushes forth. The basic image is that of moving water, continuous and powerful, that never stops. The word belongs to the family of terms describing liquid movement in Hebrew.
H5599A.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Job's discourse: in Job 14:19. Job describes how flowing water wears away the stone and carries off the earth, to illustrate that, similarly, human suffering and time slowly but inexorably wear away human hope. The context is that of the fragility of human life in the face of the forces of nature and fate.
H5599A.portee: This passage reminds the believer that the powers of the world, like the relentless current of waters, often seem to destroy what is dear to us — our health, our plans, our hope. Job forces us to face this reality; the Christian can hear that only trust in God, which endures beyond these visible destructions, allows us to bear these realities.

sens: Grains that sprout after a harvest, without having been intentionally sown
The spontaneous harvest produced by a field left to itself
What grows naturally from year to year, without the farmer's work
H5599B.detail:
1. The word refers to the ears or grains that grow of their own accord after the harvest, from fallen or remaining grains in the field. It is an involuntary growth, not sown by the farmer: in Leviticus 25:5, during the sabbatical year, one cannot harvest "what will come from the grains fallen from your harvest."
2. By extension, it refers to any harvest produced by a field without human intervention — neither sowing nor cultivation. In Leviticus 25:11, in the year of jubilee, one must not "harvest what the fields will produce of themselves."
3. Figuratively, it represents what comes naturally, without effort. In 2 Kings 19:29 and Isaiah 37:30, God promises food "that grows of itself" for two years as a sign of divine deliverance, showing that God sustains without the need for ordinary work.
H5599B.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that means "to rise" or "to emerge." It evokes the idea of what grows spontaneously, which emerges without being planted. The root is used to describe any involuntary growth — wheat that regrows, grass that grows without being sown.
H5599B.emploi: This word appears four times in the Old Testament, always in contexts of rest for the land or divine deliverance. In Leviticus 25:5 and 25:11, it is at the heart of the law of the sabbath and the jubilee: the land itself must enjoy a year of rest every seven years, during which the spontaneous productions belong to the poor and the foreigners, not to the owner. In 2 Kings 19:29 and Isaiah 37:30 (the same discourse of Isaiah to King Hezekiah), the word serves as a prophetic sign: for two years, the people will eat the regrowth of the devastated fields, proof that God will restore the land and allow a normal harvest in the third year. It is a vocabulary of dependence on God.
H5599B.portee: This word teaches that the land does not belong to the farmer absolutely: it needs rest, and its fertility comes from God alone. During the sabbath and the jubilee, the free regrowth reminds us that God feeds His people without human intervention — a lesson in trust. For the besieged King Hezekiah, it becomes a promise: even devastated, the field will produce again, proof of God's power and faithfulness.
